standard.title: Contributions to First Nations Rights
standard.description: the contributions of significant individuals and groups in the campaign for the recognition of the rights of First Nations Australians and the extent to which they brought change to Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the legislative framework of exclusion, early organised campaigns, and the Stolen Generations in K09. They understand the model of organised political activism established by the AAPA, AAL, and the 1938 Day of Mourning. They have not yet examined the specific contributions of individuals across the broader campaign period, the role of allied groups (Christian, union, labour), or the extent-of-change question.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the contributions of significant individuals and groups in the campaign for First Nations rights and evaluate the extent to which they brought change to Australian society.

nodes.label: Framework for evaluating individual and group contributions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply a framework for evaluating the contribution of individuals and groups to social change — distinguishing types of contribution and criteria for assessing extent of change.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two criteria for evaluating the contribution of an individual or group to social change and apply them to one example.
nodes.typical_width: Students establish criteria for evaluating contribution — what kinds of action produce change (legislation, public opinion, direct action, legal challenge, cultural influence)? how do we assess extent of change (what changed, how durably, how broadly)? apply criteria to one named individual before proceeding to comparison; explain the difference between contribution to change and the achievement of change — individuals rarely produce change alone.
wider: Examine the historiographical debate over the role of individuals versus structural forces in producing social change — applying this to the First Nations rights context to ask: would the 1967 Referendum have happened without specific individuals, or were structural conditions ripe regardless?
Investigate the role of oral history in documenting the contributions of First Nations activists — examining how oral sources capture dimensions of the movement that written records miss
nodes.hinge_reason: The extent-of-change evaluation in the progression endpoint requires explicit criteria. Students who lack this framework either praise all contributions uncritically or reduce the question to 'who was most famous.' Without criteria, they cannot evaluate the extent to which individuals brought change — which is the descriptor's central analytical demand.

response_modes.reason: The 'extent to which they brought change' question requires explicit scaffolding. Making the criteria concrete — type of action, durability of change, breadth of impact, connection to specific legislative or social outcomes — is the prerequisite for genuine evaluation rather than narrative description.

success_criteria: Explains at least two criteria for evaluating an individual or group's contribution to social change
Applies criteria to one named individual and produces an evaluative claim — not merely a description
Distinguishes contribution to change from sole causation of change

nodes.label: Significant individuals — selected contributions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the contributions of at least three significant individuals to the campaign for First Nations rights, applying the evaluation framework from N1.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the contributions of at least three named individuals, applying the N1 criteria to evaluate each.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate a selection of significant individuals across the campaign period — choosing from: William Cooper, Fred Maynard, Jack Patten, Charles Perkins, Vincent Lingiari, Eddie Koiki Mabo, Lowitja O'Donoghue, Neville Bonner, Gary Foley, Michael Anderson; explain what each contributed, through what means, and what changed as a result; apply the N1 framework to evaluate each contribution; examine at least one male and one female contributor, and at least one pre-1967 and one post-1967 figure.
wider: Examine the contributions of women activists — including Gladys Elphick, Essie Coffey, Joyce Clague, Daisy Bindi, Shirley Smith — analysing how their contributions have been less documented than men's and what this reveals about gendered patterns in historical memory

Investigate the role of non-Indigenous Australians who contributed to First Nations rights — examining the motivations and effectiveness of allied advocates and what their involvement reveals about the movement's breadth
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The documentation gap for women activists is a rich methodological question — why are their contributions less recorded, and what does this reveal about whose contributions historical records tend to capture? This connects directly to AC9HH10S03 and S06 skills.

response_modes.reason: Students need sufficient knowledge of multiple individuals before the comparative evaluation in N3 is meaningful. Building a repertoire of at least three contributions across different periods and methods prevents the reductive focus on one or two famous figures.

success_criteria: Explains the contributions of at least three named individuals with specific evidence
Applies the N1 evaluation criteria to at least two of the three individuals
Covers at least one pre-1967 and one post-1967 figure

nodes.label: Significant groups — organisations, allied movements, and coalitions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the contributions of significant groups — First Nations organisations and allied groups — and evaluate how coalition-building contributed to the effectiveness of the campaign.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the contribution of at least two groups — at least one First Nations organisation and one allied group; explain how coalition-building strengthened the campaign.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate First Nations organisations — the AAPA, Australian Aborigines League, Student Action for Aborigines, the Federal Council for the Advancement of Aboriginals and Torres Strait Islanders (FCAATSI); examine allied groups — Christian churches, trade unions, labour movement; explain the role of the 1938 National Day of Mourning as an organisational achievement; evaluate how coalition-building between First Nations activists and allied groups strengthened the 1967 Referendum campaign specifically.
wider: Examine the tension within the movement between working with allied non-Indigenous groups and maintaining First Nations leadership and agenda — analysing how different activists navigated this tension

Investigate the role of the trade union movement in First Nations rights — examining the Wave Hill Walk-Off as a case where labour rights and land rights intersected, and how the union movement's support both helped and complicated the campaign

response_modes.reason: Examining both First Nations organisations and allied groups gives a fuller and more accurate picture of how the campaign operated. The coalition dimension — how different groups with different motivations worked together — is analytically important for evaluating the extent of change in N4.

success_criteria: Explains the contribution of at least one First Nations organisation and one allied group
Explains how coalition-building between First Nations activists and allied groups strengthened the campaign
Identifies at least one tension or limitation in coalition relationships

nodes.label: Extent of change — evaluation and limits
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the extent to which individuals and groups brought change to Australian society — identifying what changed, how durably, and what limits remained.
nodes.minimum_width: Students construct an evaluative claim about the extent of change produced by the campaign, identifying at least one significant change and one significant limit.
nodes.typical_width: Students draw on N1–N3 to evaluate the overall extent of change — what legislative, political, and social changes resulted from individual and group contributions; what limits remained (ongoing inequality, structural racism, incomplete land rights recognition); evaluate whether changes were durable or partial; connect to K11's content on specific events and methods, and K13's content on continuing struggles — using these to calibrate the extent-of-change judgement.
wider: Evaluate the 1967 Referendum as the clearest single measure of the campaign's success — analysing what it actually changed constitutionally and what it did not change in practice
Assess the long-term impact of specific individuals on Australian society — arguing which contribution had the most durable effect and why, using the N1 criteria
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The gap between constitutional change (1967 Referendum) and practical change in lived conditions is one of the most analytically important questions in this unit — it requires students to evaluate the relationship between formal legal change and social reality, which is a transferable historical thinking skill.

response_modes.reason: This node draws together the individual contributions (N2), group contributions (N3), and the evaluation framework (N1) into a coherent judgement about extent of change. Structured argument tasks requiring students to use evidence from all three prior nodes work well here.

success_criteria: Constructs an evaluative claim about the extent of change — identifying what changed, how durably, and what limits remained
Uses evidence from at least two individuals or groups to support the claim
Identifies at least one way formal change (legislation, referendum) did not translate into full practical change
